description.cancellation_policy:
Change Policy

  • The permit is non-transferable. 
  • The permittee must be on the trip and carrying the permit at all times.
  • The group size can be reduced or increased prior to printing your permit. Please note that increases in group size will only be accommodated up to the availability for the permitted entry day for your group. Group size reductions must be made at least 7 days prior to the reserved Entry Date to receive a refund of the Special Area Fee. 

Cancellation Policy

  • The $6 reservation fee is non-refundable. As a courtesy to other users, please cancel your permit or reduce your group size as needed to free up spots for other hikers. 
  • The Special Area Fee is refundable only if cancellation or group size reduction occurs at least 7 days prior to the reserved Entry Date.
description.description:
IMPORTANT: Before purchasing a permit for the Lost Coast Trail, you must CHECK THE TIDES for your preferred dates to ensure PASSABLE TIDE WINDOWS (see "Tides" below).  

The Bureau of Land Management's (BLM) King Range Wilderness is a spectacular meeting of land and sea, as its mountains seem to thrust straight out of the surf, a dramatic rise rarely surpassed on the continental U.S. coastline. King Peak, the highest point at 4,088 feet, is only three miles from the ocean. The landscape is too rugged for highways and accessible by only a few rural roads, earning its name, “The Lost Coast”. The King Range Wilderness offers 85 miles of backpacking opportunities on trails that traverse upland mountain ridges, coastal bluffs, and beaches. The world-famous Lost Coast Trail runs 25 miles between Shelter Cove and Petrolia, CA.   Visit the King Range NCA website and use the Trip Planning Guide and the updated topographic Map to plan your visit. 

Tides must be checked for your preferred dates, prior to purchasing a permit for the Lost Coast Trail. See the Guide to Tide Safety and Tide Safety Video for instructions on how to use the NOAA website to plan your itinerary for passable tide windows. Find impassable zones on the King Range topographic Map .    

Impassable Zones & Tide Level Thresholds: On a normal day, there are 3 trail sections where the tide must be under a specific threshold (in feet) to ensure safe passage. In these “impassable zones”, the beach is very narrow, there are large boulders to traverse, and no grassy bluffs for refuge—mostly vertical bedrock walls. If the tide is too high, there is nowhere to escape the dangerous North Coast waves. 

          Zone 1: Punta Gorda (¼ mile): passable under ~6 ft. tide. 

          Zone 2: Sea Lion Gulch to Randall Cr. (4 miles): passable under 2.5 ft. tide. 

          Zone 3: Miller Cr. to Gitchell Cr. (4.5 miles): passable under 3 ft. tide. 

Always enter the impassable zones on a receding tide and plan travel at 1mph.   

 Impassable Dates 2026: Tides don't fall low enough to allow passage along the Lost Coast Trail:

July 23

August 7, 8, 20, 21, 22

September 4, 5, 6, 7, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21

October 2, 3, 4, 5, 16, 17, 28, 28, 30

November 1, 2, 14, 15, 16, 17, 28, 29, 30

December 13, 14, 15, 16, 27

The BLM does not recommend hiking at night due to inherent dangers like slippery boulders, wildlife, large waves, etc. 

Check Marine Forecast & Weather prior to your trip:

There have been many accidents, close calls, and deaths due to poor planning for impassable zones, marine conditions, and unfavorable weather. BLM does not have a search & rescue team. Proper planning is imperative.

Earthquakes & Tsunami

If a strong earthquake occurs while you are on the beach, move to higher ground immediately! The Lost Coast is home to the Mendocino Triple Junction near Cape Mendocino and is one of the most seismically active regions in California.
description.driving_directions:
The King Range NCA Visitor Center is located at: 

768 Shelter Cove Road in Whitethorn, CA. (Physical address) 

P.O. Box 189 (Mailing address)

Whitethorn, California 95589

(707) 986-5400 

Call for current road conditions see the Roads and Trails Report for specifics. Plan extra travel time due to narrow and winding roads. High clearance vehicles with 4-wheel drive are required on dirt/gravel roads in the area including King Range Rd., Smith-Etter Rd., Prosper Ridge Rd., and Windy Point Rd. Please be aware that these backcountry roads can be severely damaged when vehicles without 4-wheel drive traverse them due to spinning tires and lack of traction. There are no tow-truck companies nearby, and rescue/extraction could take many days. After high winds or storms these roads may become impassable. Please plan accordingly. 

King Range NCA Visitor Center Hours: Monday-Saturday 8:00am-4:30pm through Labor Day weekend. Closed federal holidays.
description.fee_policy:
Reservation Fee & Special Area Fee

For individuals and family groups:

  • Reservation Fee: $6 per permit

  • Special Area Fee*: $12 per person, per trip (No fee for youth under 16)

Special Recreation Permit (SRP): Organized and Commercial group fees

  • Organized group fee: $7 per person, per day  

  • Commercial group fee: 3% of total gross earnings

  • Commercial group fee (institutional): $7 per person, per day

  • Special Area Fee*: $12 per person, per trip (No fee for youth under 16)

There is a minimum $130 fee for all SRP groups. A deposit is due with submission of the application. 

For more SRP Information and to request information on how to apply for an SRP, call the King Range Visitor Center (707) 986-5400.

*The King Range Wilderness Special Area Fee is new and based on King Range Business Plan, 2024 and Federal Register Notice. Fees remain in King Range Wilderness to assist maintenance, stewardship and education.
description.need_to_know_email:
Congratulations on your upcoming trip to the King Range National Conservation Area (NCA)!  

You are required to carry a paper copy of your permit, which can be printed starting seven days before your start date.  

By printing your permit, you confirm your trip in Recreation.gov and indicate to rangers that you'll be on the trail.   

Always check current Fire Restrictions prior to visiting the King Range NCA. Usually starting in July, campfires will not be allowed anywhere in the King Range Wilderness (even on the beach, in fog). Campstoves are sometimes banned as well. Laws will be enforced and fines will apply.  

You are responsible to Educate everyone entering on your permit about important regulations, safety information, and Leave No Trace Principles. See the Trip Planning Guide , Tide Safety Guide , and Tide Safety Video  

Human Waste Disposal: When camping along the beach, bury all human waste 6-8" deep in the wet sand below the high tide line. On all other trails dig a 6-8" deep hole at least 200 ft from streams, trails, and campsites. Pack out or bury all toilet paper. Human waste has been a big issue on the Lost Coast Trail. Please clean up after yourself!

Bear-Proof Food Storage Required: Each person must use an approved hard-sided bear-resistant storage container. Food, toiletries, trash, dog food, and other scented items must be secured in container when not in use.  

Dogs are not recommended: Unless a seasoned backpacking dog, due to injuries to paws on sharp, hot rocks. Leashes are required between Punta Gorda and Sea Lion Gulch at all times. 

Avoid Elephant Seal Colony between Windy Point & lighthouse, move to the upper bluff trail and off the beach, observe from above. Do not disturb seals. Remain at least 100 ft away.

DO NOT build driftwood structures, they become homes for rattlesnakes and rodents.

Beware of Ocean! Swimming, wading & skim boarding are not safe due to strong undertow & sneaker waves. Many lives have been lost.

Have a wonderful adventure!
description.need_to_know_order:
Please carefully read the information below and click the check box to agree to our Rules and Regulations for King Range Wilderness Permits.

I understand:

  • Hiking the Lost Coast Trail and King Range Wilderness requires a large amount of planning and research. It is my responsibility to learn about its unique challenges including ocean safety, tide thresholds, impassable dates and locations, water availability & filtration, weather advisories, marine forecasting, communication services, campfire restrictions, etc.  

  • As the Permit Holder, I am responsible to educate my guests on all rules, regulations, and safety concerns. This is where groups often fall short and when accidents occur. 

  • Organized or Commercial groups need a Special Recreation Permit. My trip is not for a business, outfitter, non-profit, scout troop, meet-up group, non-profit, school, etc. If my group is in fact one of these groups or if I need additional information, I will not purchase this permit and instead research Special Recreation Permits.

As the Permit Holder, I agree to:

1) Enter only on my exact ENTRY DATE with the exact # of PEOPLE, as allowed on this permit.  

2) Watch the Tide Safety Video , prior to purchasing this permit to ensure tide windows. I understand that many dates are impassible on the LCT.

3) Print and carry my permit to present to park rangers. Printing instructions will be in my confirmation email.

4) Follow all Fire Restrictions including: NO CAMPFIRES annually between June 19 and September 30.

5) Follow all rules, regulations, and guidelines for the King Range Wilderness including those on my printed permit and on the King Range website & Trip Planning Guide .  

6) Make changes or cancel my permit at least 7 days before my entry date to free up permits for others.

7) Learn and strictly follow Leave No Trace Principles including proper backcountry bathroom practices.

8) Educate myself and guests about Staying Safe on North Coast Beaches. It is never safe to swim or wade in the ocean.
description.need_to_know_permit:
Important Safety & Trip Planning Info:

Impassable Zones

ALERT: There are 3 sections on the Lost Coast Trail that are impassable at certain tide levels. 

#1: Punta Gorda--passable under 6 ft 

#2: Sea Lion Gulch to Randall Creek--passable under 2.5 ft 

#3: Miller Flat to Gitchell Creek--passable under 3 ft  

Before purchasing permits, watch Tide Safety Video . Properly plan your trip itinerary to ensure your safety and ability to pass, PRIOR to purchasing a permit.   

“Low tide” does NOT EQUAL “passable”. There are dates that the low tide does not fall under the passable threshold. In other words, just because its “LOW TIDE”, it doesn’t mean the trail is safe to pass. Always use the above thresholds to determine a passable tide window through each impassable zone.   

DO NOT ASSUME that if permits are for sale, the dates are passable on LCT. These permits are for the entire King Range Wilderness, including the upland trails. 

Watch the ocean! Especially on sloped beaches, avoid walking near the water because forceful waves can surge up at any time without notice (sneaker waves). The ocean on the Lost Coast can sweep a person off their feet, out to sea, and to their death at any time.  

Never attempt to swim or wade on this stretch of the Pacific Ocean due to strong undertow and rip currents. The water is very cold, and survival is often limited to 20 minutes without a wetsuit. Don’t ever assume it is ok to “just get a bit wet” to pass through impassable zones. 

Weather can change drastically; be prepared with a backup plan. From October thru April, the King Range Wilderness is one of the wettest spots in the U.S. with annual rainfall averaging 120 inches. Storms can make coastal creeks impassable very fast. Never attempt to cross creeks above knee height. Wait for water to subside. 

Check the marine forecast just before your trip. Find the forecast for Cape Mendocino to Point Arena. Note the winds, wave height, and period/seconds.   

Campfire Permit is REQUIRED! A campfire permit is required from CAL FIRE to operate camp stoves and campfires. Find Campfire Permit here. 

Hard-sided Bear Canisters are required. The canister must be of appropriate size to store all scented items including food, soap, sunscreen, and trash. Each person must possess a minimum of one canister. Bags are not allowed. Visitors failing to use hard-sided canisters are subject to fines (43 CFR 8365.1-6). Bear can rental provided at the King Range Visitor Center. 

Drinking Water is usually available in year-round coastal creeks and springs. Always treat your water using an approved filtration method or by boiling it. Water sources may be scarce along upland trails, so bring plenty of water, especially in dry years. 

Other Hazards Ticks, poison oak, and rattlesnakes are common. Be able to identify and avoid them. Poison oak grows all over the KRNCA in many forms—vines on trees, bushes along coast bluffs, and even small waxy plants in the sand. Ticks are also present, especially in spring/early summer. Rattlesnakes hide under large driftwood and sometimes lay on the trail. Avoid all these hazards by remaining aware of your surroundings.  

Dogs are not recommended.

Frequently Asked Questions

  • Do I have to start my hike on the Entry Date listed on my permit? Yes, the correct Entry Date is required, no exceptions.  

  • Do I need a permit for day use in the King Range Wilderness? No, permits are required for overnight use only.

  • Can I transfer my permit to another person? No, permits are non-transferable. 

  • How do I cancel my permit if I decide to not go? Cancel on Recreation.gov account.  Reservation fee is non-refundable. Wilderness Area fee is only refundable if at least 7 days prior to entry date.

  • How many people can hike together in a group? All organized and commercial groups need a Special Recreation Permit, no exceptions. Max. SRP size=15.   

  • Why should I check the marine forecast in addition to the weather? Weather, wind, and ocean swells may affect the ability to traverse safely on the LCT. A large swell can shorten the amount of time to get through a tidal zone safely. Long period secondary swells can mean an increased likelihood of sneaker waves. This can mean life or death-hazardous ocean conditions have resulted in hikers being swept out to sea.

  • Can I swim in the ocean? No. Never ever swim, wade, or use skim boards in the ocean anywhere on the Lost Coast due to rip currents, strong undertow, and sneaker waves.  

  • Who is responsible for making sure our group is safe on the LCT? It is your duty as a permit holder to ensure each person on your permit is aware of all rules & safety concerns. The BLM does NOT have a Search & Rescue team. Assume self-extrication. Carry In-Reach device for extreme emergencies.

  • Who is checking permits? Rangers at the trailheads and on trail. 

  • Are hard-sided bear canisters are required? Yes, bear cans are required. Bear bags/hangs are NOT acceptable. Cans are available for rent in several King Range locations.

  • Where do I use the bathroom on the LCT? Deposit solid human waste in a hole dug 6" deep in the intertidal zone. Never go near backcountry campsites. In uplands, 200 feet from fresh water, camp, and trails. Always pack out your toilet paper in your bear can.

  • How deep are the creek crossings? Heavy rainfall will cause water levels in the creek to rise to unsafe levels. Do not cross if over knee high. Be prepared for changing weather and call visitor center for current conditions. 

  • Can I have a campfire? It depends on the time of year. You must have a CalFire Campfire permit in addition to a Wilderness Permit. Use existing campfire rings and always put fire out before bed or leaving site. Campfires are prohibited July through October.  

  • Can I bring my drone in the wilderness and Lost Coast Trail? DRONES are NOT allowed. 

  • Additional Information here: https://www.recreation.gov/permits/445864/additional-information

  • King Range Visitor Center Hours: Monday-Saturday 8:00am-4:30pm through Labor Day weekend. Closed federal holidays.
description.no_show_policy: Please cancel your permit if you end up not using it so that others may enjoy the wilderness.
description.quota_details:
In the King Range Wilderness, a permit quota system has been set up to ensure visitors a wilderness experience free of large crowds and an opportunity for solitude. The sale of daily entry permits sets a limit to the number of people that may enter each day. Permits are required year-round for overnight use. 

Permittees MUST ENTER the wilderness on the EXACT ENTRY DATE printed on the permit. No exceptions! Rangers will check permits on the trail or at the trailhead.  

Individual Wilderness Permits may include entry for up to 3 people. Each permittee may have one active permit at a time.    

The quota system limits trailhead entrees within the King Range Wilderness to:

  • 60 persons per day, May 15 through September 15 

  • 30 persons per day, September 16 through May 14 

DO NOT ASSUME that if permits are for sale, the tide windows on the Lost Coast Trail are safe. The quota system and permit sales are for the King Range Wilderness, not only the Lost Coast Trail.
description.season_information:
Wilderness permits are required for overnight use in the King Range Wilderness. Day use does not require a permit. 

Permits are available on an a 90-day rolling reservation system and may be reserverd 90-days prior to entry at 7:00 am PST. For example: on 10/1/25, permits will open for 1/1/26; on 10/2/25 for 1/2/26, etc. Permittees are allowed one active permit at a time.   

Organized and Commercial groups must obtain a Special Recreation Permit (i.e. outfitters, scout troops, schools, etc.). The maximum group size is 15 people.

Walk up permits for up to 3 starts (people) are available at the King Range Visitor Center by lottery which will be conducted Mon-Sat at 8:00am. Walk up permits that are still available after the lottery will be issued first come/first served.

Permit isn’t officially issued until printed. The permit must be carried by the permittee. You may print your permit 7 days before your entry date. Once your permit has been printed, you cannot make changes.
description.tertiary_page:
King Range Wilderness Permits (Lost Coast)

Camp Zone Descriptions and Map

The camp zone descriptions and mapare intended to assist in planning your overnight backcountry trip into the King Range Wilderness.

For more information we suggest contacting the King Range Project Office at (707) 986-5400. 

Camp Zone Area Descriptions:

  • North Coast: Lost Coast Trail from the Mattole Trailhead to Cooskie Creek

  • Uplands North: King Range Wilderness above the Lost Coast Trail from Mattole Trailhead to the north end of Big Flat

  • Randall-Spanish-Big Creeks: Lost Coast Trail from Randall Creek to the north end of Big Flat

  • Big Flat/Miller Flat: Lost Coast Trail on the north and south side of Big Flat Creek

  • Buck and Shipman Creeks: Lost Coast Trail from the south end of Miller Flat to approximately 0.5 mile south of Buck Creek

  • Uplands South: King Range Wilderness above the Lost Coast Trail from the north end of Big Flat to Lightning Trailhead and extending south to Shelter Cove

  • South Coast: One mile north of Gitchell Creek to Black Sands Beach Trailhead

  • Chemise Mountain: King Range Wilderness south of Shelter Cove; Hidden Valley Trailhead to Sinkyone Wilderness State Park

Additional Information:

Dogs are not recommended on the Lost Coast Trail: Dogs are often injure their paws on the sharp, hot rocks. It’s also a difficult walk over long boulder fields along the coast. Many owners have been forced to carry their dogs out due to injuries. Leashes are always required between Punta Gorda and Sea Lion Gulch due to the elephant seals.

Avoid Elephant Seal Colony between Windy Point & Punta Gorda lighthouse. Move to the upper bluff trail and off the beach, observe from above. Do not disturb seals. Remain at least 100 ft away. Watch for seals laying on and around the trail and move away from them. Please do not attempt to take selfies with them. Seals that feel threatened will return to the cold water prior to growing back fur and will perish due to cold. Harbor seals are even more suseptable to this consequence. 

DO NOT build driftwood structures, they become homes for rattlesnakes and rodents.

Beware of Ocean! Swimming, wading & skim boarding are not safe due to strong undertow & sneaker waves. Many lives have been lost along this stretch of coastline. 

Human Waste Disposal: When camping along the Lost Coast Trail, bury all human waste 6-8" deep in the wet sand below the high tide line in the intertidal zone. Take the extra walk to the beach like everyone else, to keep the small, confined campsites sanitary over the summer. Human waste has been a big issue on the Lost Coast Trail. Please be respectful of our wilderness. On upland trails dig a 6-8" deep hole at least 200 ft from streams, trails, and campsites. Pack out toilet paper. 

Did you check the tides before you purchased this permit? Did you read that there are many dates in which the Lost Coast Trail is NOT passable at all because the low tide doesn’t get retreat under the safe threshold? Go back to the “Need to Know” section where you purchased this permit on Recreation.gov.

Always check current Fire Restrictions prior to visiting the KRNCA. Usually starting in July, campfires will not be allowed anywhere in the King Range Wilderness (even on the beach, in fog). Camp stoves are sometimes banned as well. Laws will be enforced, and fines will apply.  

You are responsible to educate everyone entering on your permit about important regulations, safety information, and Leave No Trace Principles. See the Trip Planning Guide, Tide Safety Guide , and Tide Safety Video. Why not send a quick email with these links so they can read the information for themselves?

Bear-Proof Food Storage Required: Each person must use an approved hard-sided bear-resistant storage container. Food, toiletries, trash, dog food, sunscreen, and other scented items must be secured in container when not in use.  

Please be safe, help us by leaving no trace of your visit in the wilderness, and have a wonderful adventure!  

Leave No Trace Principles- the 7 Principles must be applied in the King Range NCA and Lost Coast Trail. See "Trip Planning Guide" for site specific info.

  • Plan ahead and prepare: research tides, campsites, mileage, what to bring, weather, etc.

  • Travel and camp on durable surfaces: reduce impacts by using established trails and campsites. Good campsites are found, not made.

  • Dispose of waste properly: where do you poop? On LCT, bury 6" deep in the intertidal zone. DO NOT POOP near campsites! On ridges, dig hole 200ft from waterways and camp.

  • Leave what you find: leave rocks, plants, and natural objects as you find them, for the next person to see.

  • Minimize campfire impacts: check for campfire restrictions. Always use fire ring or camp stove. Put out fire completely and scatter cool ashes.

  • Respect wildlife: observe all wildlife from a distance. DO NOT FEED any animals. Avoid elephant seals near lighthouse.

  • Be considerate of others: respect others and their wilderness experience.

445864001.description: Visitors planning to camp overnight in the King Range Wilderness will be asked to provide a tentative itinerary; including number of days in the wilderness, entrance trailhead, exit trailhead, and backcountry camp zones. To assist in planning an overnight trip into the King Range Wilderness, take time to review the trailhead descriptions and directions , as we ll as the camp zone map and zone descriptions . Permittees are required to watch this video on tide planning: https://youtu.be/GGILd6ZWw0k. The start date of the permit is strictly monitored and visitors are required to begin their trip on the permitted start date. Early or late starts will not be authorized. Permit availability is based on the start date only.
